options.tagChildHint: The bottom number tells you how many slices the cake is cut into. If you cut it into more slices, what happens to the size of each slice?
The top numbers match, so look at the bottoms. Smaller bottoms make bigger pieces.
Any two fractions can be compared. Draw each one and see which covers more.

rows.walkScript: Give both fractions the same bottom number first. That makes 4/5 into 36/45 and 4/9 into 20/45. So 4/5 is the bigger share. One trap thinks a bigger bottom means a bigger piece.

stem.text: What is 2/3 of 18?

options.tagChildHint: You found part of it. Now read the question again and finish.
Check which number is on top. Turning it over changes the fraction.
A fraction is two numbers working together. Use both.

rows.walkScript: Find one third of 18 first. Share 18 into three, giving 6 each. Two thirds means two of those parts, so 12. Some traps stop at one part or flip the fraction.

stem.text: In Bag A, 1/3 of the marbles are red. In Bag B, the marbles are red and blue in the ratio 1 : 3. Which bag has the greater fraction of red marbles?

options.tagChildHint: The bottom number tells you how many slices the cake is cut into. If you cut it into more slices, what happens to the size of each slice?
A fraction is part of the whole. First, add the ratio parts to find the total.
Any two fractions can be compared. Draw each one and see which covers more.

rows.walkScript: Bag B splits into 1 red for every 3 blue. That means 1 red in every 4 marbles, so 1/4. Bag A holds 1/3, which is more than 1/4. A trap reads the ratio as the fraction itself.

stem.text: What is 1/5 written as a decimal?

options.tagChildHint: 0.3 means three-tenths (3/10). Does one-third equal three-tenths?
A fraction is two numbers working together. Use both.
A fraction is a single number. The line in the middle just means "divide".

rows.walkScript: One fifth means one whole shared into five. Ten tenths shared into five gives two tenths each. So 1/5 is 0.2. A trap copies a digit from the fraction instead.

stem.text: There are 48 sweets in a jar. 25% of them are eaten. How many sweets are left?

options.tagChildHint: 50% is a half. 25% is exactly half of that, which makes it one quarter!
Percent means "out of 100". The percent is a share of the amount, not a number to take away from it!
You found the discount, well done! Now subtract it from the starting price to finish.

rows.walkScript: First find 25% of 48, which is a quarter. A quarter of 48 is 12 sweets eaten. Take 12 from 48 to leave 36. A trap stops at the eaten amount, or halves instead.

stem.text: A bottle holds 6 litres of water. Each glass holds 2/3 of a litre. How many glasses can be filled?

options.tagChildHint: Ask how many fit inside. That is a sharing question, not a times.
Each bag or glass holds only part of one kilogram or litre. So do not count one bag or glass for each kilogram or litre.
A fraction is two numbers working together. Use both.

rows.walkScript: You are asking how many 2/3 litres fit in 6. Flip the two thirds and multiply: 6 times 3/2. That fills 9 glasses. A trap multiplies by the fraction, making it smaller.

stem.text: A jug is 1/3 full of juice. Then another 1/4 of a jug is poured in. What fraction of the jug is now full?

options.tagChildHint: You can only add fractions when the bottom numbers are exactly the same. Find a common denominator first.
Whatever you multiply the top by, you need to multiply the bottom by too.
You found part of it. Now read the question again and finish.

rows.walkScript: Give both fractions the same bottom number, twelfths. That turns 1/3 into 4/12 and 1/4 into 3/12. Add the tops to get 7/12. A trap adds tops and bottoms straight across.

stem.text: A coat costs £64. In a sale it is reduced by 25%. What is the sale price?

options.tagChildHint: Percent means "out of 100". The percent is a share of the amount, not a number to take away from it!
You found part of it. Now read the question again and finish.
50% is a half. 25% is exactly half of that, which makes it one quarter!

rows.walkScript: A quarter off means find one quarter of sixty-four pounds. Take that discount away from the sixty-four. The sale price is £48. The trap halves it, adds the percent, or stops.

stem.text: A rectangle is 18 cm long and 9 cm wide. What is its perimeter?

options.tagChildHint: Walk all the way round the shape. Count every side once.
To find the perimeter, imagine walking around the very edge. Add up the whole journey.
Cross out your carried number once you add it. This stops you from counting it again.

rows.walkScript: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Add a long side and a short side. Then double that total to reach 54 cm. One trap swaps in the area instead.

stem.text: Two angles sit together on a straight line. One angle is 137°. What is the size of the other angle?

options.tagChildHint: First ask what the angles make: a straight line, a triangle or a full turn. A line and a triangle both make 180°, and a full turn makes 360°.
Always take the bottom digit from the top. If the top is smaller, exchange.
If the top column does not have enough, you need to exchange from the next one.

rows.walkScript: Angles on a straight line always add to 180. Take the 137 away from 180. The angle left is 43 degrees. One trap uses the full-turn total.

stem.text: On a grid, a counter is at point (5, 2). It is moved 6 squares right and 4 squares up. What are the new coordinates of the counter?

options.tagChildHint: Go along the corridor (x) before you go up the stairs (y).
Do not count the point you start on. Each jump to the next grid line counts as one square.
Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.

rows.walkScript: Read along the corridor, then up the stairs. Six right takes 5 to 11. Four up takes 2 to 6. The counter lands at (11, 6); one trap slides the other way.

stem.text: A rectangle has an area of 48 cm² and a length of 8 cm. First find its width, then work out its perimeter.

options.tagChildHint: Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.
Walk all the way round the shape. Count every side once.
You found part of it. Now read the question again and finish.

rows.walkScript: Area is length times width, so width is 48 shared by 8, giving 6 cm. Now add 8 and 6, then double for the perimeter. That makes 28 cm. One trap stops at the width. Another adds only three sides.

stem.text: An L-shape is made from a rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm. A corner 5 cm by 4 cm is cut out. What is the area of the L-shape?

options.tagChildHint: Find the area of the whole block first, then subtract the piece that was cut away.
Perimeter is the fence around the outside (add the sides). Area is the grass inside (multiply the length by the width).
Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.

rows.walkScript: Find the whole block first: 12 times 8 is 96. The cut-out corner is 5 times 4, which is 20. Take the cut-out away to leave 76 cm². One trap forgets the cut-out.

stem.text: A triangle rests on a straight line. One angle of the triangle sits next to an angle of 140° on that line. Another angle of the triangle is 30°. What is the third angle of the triangle?

options.tagChildHint: You found part of it. Now read the question again and finish.
First ask what the angles make: a straight line, a triangle or a full turn. A line and a triangle both make 180°, and a full turn makes 360°.
Check that an angle is inside the triangle before you use it. Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.

rows.walkScript: The straight line gives the inside angle: 180 take 140 is 40. A triangle's angles add to 180. Take away 40 and 30 to leave 110 degrees. One trap stops before the last step.

stem.text: Ravi has £8. He buys a book for £3.40. How much change does he get?

options.tagChildHint: Always line up the decimal points. Add place-holder zeros so the columns match perfectly.
Words like "change" or "left" usually mean subtraction. Take the amount away instead of adding.
Count on to the next pound, then on to the money given. Add both jumps to find the change.

rows.walkScript: Change means you line the amounts up and subtract. Write £8 as £8.00 so the pence match. Take £3.40 away to leave £4.60. A trap adds the prices or drops the pence.

stem.text: A bag of flour weighs 4000 g. What is its mass in kilograms?

options.tagChildHint: A metre is much larger than a centimetre, so you will need fewer of them. If you are going to a larger unit, you need to divide.
"Kilo" always means one thousand. There are 1,000 grams in a kilogram.
One hundred has two zeros. Make sure you divide by 100, not a different number.

rows.walkScript: A kilogram is much heavier than a gram. There are 1,000 grams in every kilogram. So share 4,000 by 1,000 to get 4 kg. A trap multiplies, or divides by a smaller number.

stem.text: Anya buys a ruler for £1.70 and a pen for £2.60. What is the total cost?

options.tagChildHint: Cross out your carried number once you add it. This stops you from counting it again.
Write your carried numbers clearly. Then add them to the next column.
Rounding helps you check an answer. Work the real numbers out too.

rows.walkScript: Add the two prices, pounds and pence together. Seventy pence plus sixty pence makes £1.30. That carries to give £4.30 in total. A trap loses the carried pound, or counts it as ten pounds.

stem.text: A blue rope is 74 cm long. A red rope is 29 cm long. How much longer is the blue rope?

options.tagChildHint: Words like "change" or "left" usually mean subtraction. Take the amount away instead of adding.
Always take the bottom digit from the top. If the top is smaller, exchange.
Line the digits up in their columns. Every digit needs a place.

rows.walkScript: How much longer means you find the difference. Take 29 cm away from 74 cm. That leaves 45 cm. A trap adds the two lengths instead.

stem.text: A bus leaves at 2:45 pm. The journey takes 40 minutes. What time does it arrive?

options.tagChildHint: There are only 60 minutes in an hour. Once you hit 60, you need to roll over into the next hour.
Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.
Rounding helps you check an answer. Work the real numbers out too.

rows.walkScript: First count the minutes up to the next hour. From 2:45, fifteen minutes reaches 3:00. Twenty-five minutes are left, so 3:25 pm. A trap lets the minutes pass sixty.

stem.text: One parcel weighs 375 g. Another parcel weighs 246 g. What is their total mass?

options.tagChildHint: Line the digits up in their columns. Every digit needs a place.
Write your carried numbers clearly. Then add them to the next column.
Cross out your carried number once you add it. This stops you from counting it again.

rows.walkScript: Line the digits up in their columns and add. Five plus six is eleven, so carry the ten. Keep going to reach 621 g. A trap drops a digit or a carried ten.

stem.text: Leo buys 3 pens at £1.15 each. He pays with a £5 note. How much change does he get?

options.tagChildHint: You found part of it. Now read the question again and finish.
Count the groups or steps again before you work it out. Use the exact number, not one more or one fewer.
Always line up the decimal points. Add place-holder zeros so the columns match perfectly.

rows.walkScript: First find the cost of three pens. Three times £1.15 is £3.45 spent. Take that from £5 to leave £1.55. A trap stops at the total spent.

stem.text: In the number 8,473, what is the value of the digit 4?

options.tagChildHint: Keep that digit in its column and change all the other digits to zeros. The digits after it are not part of its value.
Look at where the digit sits. Its position changes its actual value!
Check the columns carefully. Name every column, counting out from the ones. Which column does that digit actually sit in?

rows.walkScript: Find where the 4 sits. It stands in the hundreds column. So its value is four hundreds, which is 400. The trap reads a neighbouring column or its face value.

stem.text: What number is 100 more than 5,960?

options.tagChildHint: Check the columns carefully. Name every column, counting out from the ones. Which column does that digit actually sit in?
Check the columns carefully. Name every column, counting out from the ones. Which column does that digit actually sit in?
Write your carried numbers clearly. Then add them to the next column.

rows.walkScript: First find the hundreds column. Add one hundred to the nine hundreds. That makes ten hundreds, so carry into the thousands to reach 6,060. The trap adds into a neighbouring column or drops the carry.

stem.text: What number is 1,000 more than 9,500?

options.tagChildHint: Check the columns carefully. Name every column, counting out from the ones. Which column does that digit actually sit in?
Check the columns carefully. Name every column, counting out from the ones. Which column does that digit actually sit in?
Write your carried numbers clearly. Then add them to the next column.

rows.walkScript: Look at the thousands column first. Add one thousand to the nine thousands. Ten thousands form, so carry into the next column to reach 10,500. The trap adds into a neighbouring column or loses the carry.

stem.text: Round 2,673 to the nearest 100.

options.tagChildHint: Check which place the question asks for. Then look at the digit after it.
Check which place the question asks for. Then look at the digit after it.
Look at the next digit along. If it is 5 or more, round up.

rows.walkScript: Rounding to the nearest hundred means checking the tens digit. Here it is seven, so round up. 2,673 becomes 2,700. The trap rounds to a different place or chops the end off.

stem.text: In the number 7.482, what is the value of the digit 8?

options.tagChildHint: Look at where the digit sits. Its position changes its actual value!
Check the columns carefully. Name every column, counting out from the ones. Which column does that digit actually sit in?
The decimal point separates wholes from parts. Read each digit after the point in its own column, not as one whole number.

rows.walkScript: Find where the 8 sits. It stands in the hundredths column. So its value is eight hundredths, which is 0.08. The trap reads a neighbouring column or the plain digit.

stem.text: The temperature is 6°C. It falls by 10°C. What is the new temperature?

options.tagChildHint: Count down past zero. The numbers keep going on the other side.
Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.
List every number the question gives you. Check you have used each one.

rows.walkScript: Start at six and count downwards. Cross zero into the minus numbers. Ten steps down from six lands on minus four. The traps keep it positive, add instead of taking away, or forget to start from six.

stem.text: Round 4,750 to the nearest 100.

options.tagChildHint: Exactly halfway always rounds up. If it ends in 5, go up to the next number.
Check which place the question asks for. Then look at the digit after it.
Check which place the question asks for. Then look at the digit after it.

rows.walkScript: This number sits exactly halfway between two hundreds. The rule says round a halfway number up. So 4,750 becomes 4,800. The trap rounds the half down or picks another place.

stem.text: 4 pens cost 60p. How much do 6 pens cost at the same price?

options.tagChildHint: Find the cost of just one first. Then multiply that.
Multiply by how many you need now. Not by how many more.
You found one share. Now count how many you need.

rows.walkScript: Find the cost of one pen first. Share 60p by 4 to get 15p each. Six pens are 15p times 6, which is 90p. One trap scales by the extra count.

stem.text: One shop sells 5 pens for 100p. Another shop sells 4 pens for 60p. How much cheaper is one pen at the second shop than at the first?

options.tagChildHint: The packs hold different amounts. Find the price of one first.
Match each price to its own pack. Keep the pairs together.
Always take the bottom digit from the top. If the top is smaller, exchange.

rows.walkScript: Put both shops into the same form: one pen. The first shop is 20p each, the second is 15p. Take 15 from 20 to save 5p. One trap compares the packs, not the pens.

stem.text: A table shows badges won. Red team won 10, Blue team 9, Green team 14 and Yellow team 8. How many more did Green and Red win together than Blue and Yellow together?

options.tagChildHint: Double-check the chart. Have you added together every single row or bar you need?
Look at the axis labels. Are you counting the right things?
Always take the bottom digit from the top. If the top is smaller, exchange.

rows.walkScript: Add each group before you compare. Green and Red make 24; Blue and Yellow make 17. Take 17 from 24 to leave 7. One trap leaves a team out.

stem.text: In five spelling tests, Omar scored 6, 9, 7, 10 and 8. What is his mean (average) score?

options.tagChildHint: You found part of it. Now read the question again and finish.
Count how many numbers you added. Divide by that.
Mean means add them up, then share. Check which one is asked.

rows.walkScript: The mean has two steps: total, then share. Add the five scores to make 40. Share 40 between the 5 tests. The mean is 8; one trap stops before sharing.
